(e) prohibit for a stated period, or permanently, the landing in Canada, or the landing at any specified port of entry in Canada, of

immigrants belonging to any race deemed nn-suited to the climate or requirements of Canada, or of immigrants of any specified class, occupation or character.	_
Perhaps the minister will tell us what he had in mind when he drew this clause. There must be some class to which it applies specially.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have not, at the moment, any class particularly in mind, but we want to be in such a position that, should occasion arise, when public policy seems to demand it, we may have the power, on our responsibility as a government, to exclude people whom we consider undesirable. If this power is given to the government, then the government can be held responsible should there be a sudden influx of an undesirable class of people. We cannot tell at what time or under what circumstances there may be a sudden movement of people from one part of the world or another, and we want to be in a position to check it, should public policy demand such action.

I thought this would refer probably to Japanese or some of these people with whom we had so much trouble before, and when the through ticket was the cause of it being made. Under this section, parties must come direct from their own country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is provided for under subsection (a). I understood the hon. member to ask with regard to subsection (c). Subsection (a) is exactly as my hon. friend has stated.
And the other is the same.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, subsection (c) is to give the government arbitrary power to prohibit the landing of any class of people. Suppose there was a sudden influx of people from some undesirable Asiatic or African country, we could, without ceremony, simply say: You cannot land.

Under section 38 the government is given wide powers, but I must say that I personally favour giving those wide powers. Of course, the minister sees that there are two broad aspects to this question of immigration-to encourage desirable settlers, and also to prohibit those who would be undesirable. We have to steer carefully-I suppose the minister is endeavouring to do it in this Bill-to avoid undue encouragement to those who would never make desirable citizens, and yet not to prohibit too harshly those who may desire to add to our population. We seem to be framing our laws a good deal along the lines of those of the United States. We know that in the earlier years immigration to the United States was practically unchecked. v The civilization of the eastern states was strong enough to impose its character upon the larger part of the west. But the west ern states are filling up. They have received population from every part of the world, and they are experiencing difficulties and imposing checks. But their problems are not exactly the same as ours. Their lands are practically filled up, and they have not to tout for immigration. But we have our waste spaces which it is desirable to fill up with the right class of people. I offer apologies to the minister for speaking in this general way now. It would have been better to deal with these matters on the second reading of the Bill, but, unfortunately, I had no opportunity to do so. This Act on the whole certainly makes for progress along the right line. But I may say that in so far as it succeeds in prohibiting undesirable immigration, it depends entirely for its success on its administration by the executive officials. I would like to say a word as to that bonus question. I think that on the whole it is not wise to continue the bonus system. I quite appreciate the reasons the minister put up, namely, that it was in reality an advertising proposition, whereby the booking agents, although they got a bonus, reallv gave the country a c^iid pro quo in the shape of advertisements. In looking at these things in Great Britain, where I spent five months two years ago, in connection with the immigration of certain types into our own province, I had some occasion to come into contact with those people, and my own feeling is that these booking agents, who after all derive tre mendous benefits from the government advertising and the government literature, can very well afford to dispense with the bonus, and that money could be put into a more direct method of advertising on the part of the government. Tim mere fact that they get a commission in transmitting people to this country is an inducement to the booking agents to work up their business, and it may also be said that the fact that they get a bonus would certainly stimulate them perhaps to hold out encouragements of a misleading character to people. I had occasion to see a good deal of this when I was in t'he old country. Of course, I admit it was in the winter time, when there was a great depression, which favoured the efforts of these booking agents, and even of some of the government's own agents, and -when they sent large numbers of people to this country when it was not in the interest of those people that they should come.
Now, I think that the success^ of the minister's general scheme of immigration, and the success of this Act, will be de-

pendent in a large measure on the type of men that he puts on in Great Britain and other chuntries as official agents over immigration matters. My own feeling is that it requires an exceptional man to be a good agent, a broad-minded, fair-minded type of man, and not merely a man who has rendered some political service to the government, or even to the country at large, unless he is specially fitted for that sort of work. I have seen again and again many loose statements made by officials of the department who were not, I should think, qualified to speak of the general conditions in Canada in a way that would give a fair impression to people who desired to emigrate to Canada. I will give one or two instances to show the care that should be exercised in the selection of these agents. We know there is a tendency to paint everything in rosy colours before the eyes of intending immigrants, and never to show them any of the difficulties with which they are likely to be confronted. I have seen again and again statements made, in answer to inquiries, that would lead a man to come out to this country with the expectation that practically he had nothing to do but to go on to 160 acres of land, and in some mysterions way acquire a fortune without doing much of anything to earn it. There is another point. I believe that these agents should have a thorough knowledge of the whole of Canada. I was much surprised to hear a remark made by an hon. gentleman sitting in front of me, that of that enormous population in the northwest something like 440,000 were from eastern Canada. Well, if that is so, it shows a depletion going on from eastern Canada. Now, I say that the kind of immigration agent the minister should try to secure-because I take it for granted that his aim is to control the movement of immigration into all parts of Canada-is a man broad in his knowledge of facts, and with a fairly familiar acquaintance with the conditions in all parts of Canada. I know that these men have great power in their hands; and while it might be suitable and the best thing to do to direct some classes of immigrants into Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and other eastern provinces, it might be better in a great many cases to direct them to the western provinces. Bor instance, if a man wishes to go to British Columbia and seeks information regarding that province from the agent, the agent may know nothing about British Columbia. I came across a case in which one of the leading agents of the government admitted that his knowledge of Canada stopped short of the Rocky mountains, he had absolutely no knowledge except by hearsay of any of the conditions beyond the Rocky mountains. Although many inquiries were made along that line, Mr. BURRELL.
he could not answer them, he could not give these people satisfaction, and to that extent we in British Columbia were deprived of getting good settlers. Now, I am free to admit that the minister has changed his policy somewhat within the last two years. Let me quote now a remark made two or three years ago by a strong Liberal and supporter of my hon. friend's government, speaking in this House:
The federal government spent thousands of dollars in encouraging immigrants to the Northwest, but not one dollar in getting immigrants for British Columbia. Arrangements were made with transportation companies for cheap rates to the Northwest, and tli* self-same companies were allowed to compensate themeslves for these reductions by soaking those who had the courage to venture to British Columbia. So far as British Columbia was concerned, its chief function as a part of confederation was to produce revenue to be expended elsewhere in making this a great country.
I think the minister will admit that that policy was the one in force about two years ago. I am glad to say that in some directions the minister has recognized the fact that there is a considerable proportion of the population of Canada on the other side of the Rocky mountains, a region which he is endeavouring to bring to the notice of people in the old country who are suitable for its needs. Now, I think it should' be clearly understood that the building up of the western country is better done at that end, and the money expended for that purpose is best spent on men who will frankly set before the public the exact conditions as they exist. Again and again I have seen men make failures in this country because they have been absolutely misled and induced to come out here with false expectations. I have always been under the impression that so far as Canada goes the facts are good enough. The potentialities of our country are all right in themselves, if they are put before the people in the right way. Let me give another illustration of a type of immigrant that we do not want. I remember a short time ago there was a case tnat excited a good deal of interest at the time, a criminal case, in which a man who had committed some crime was being testified against by his wife, and she had made a statement in court that he was in such a deplorable state of mind that he would threaten either to drown himself or to leave Canada. 1 frankly admitted, after speaking of these things, that if any man there was putting Canada just about the drowning point, .he should not be encouraged to come to Canada, but should stay where he was. I have had young fellows come to me, and I have no doubt the government officials have had the same experience, with the most vague ideas of what coming to Canada
585?

meant. I could give one illustration where a young fellow who had been working on the stock exchange as a clerk for 12 years had a fixed desire to come to Canada, and wished particularly to come to British Columbia. When I questioned him as to what his ideas were, I found they were somewhat vague. He had read the literature, he had seen some agents, and had an idea that all he had to do was to come here to change his life to something infinitely better. When I asked him if he had any money and what his prospects were, it was so hopeless a prospect that I fankly took my courage in my hands and told him to stay where he was. I believe there is as much wisdom in agents advising people not to come to Canada in some instances as in holding out false inducements to them to come. I do not say that all the men the government have in Great Britain are men of this kind, because some of them are very good agents and are doing the best they can to give us good settlers.
We must look at the whole question of immigration in a broad way. We have an immense problem which is just hinted at by the very section which the minister has been dealing with. Those of us who are familiar with the facts know what is in the minister's mind, we know that in connection with this clause we want as far as we can to build up a type of civilization in the far west, and in Canada generally that will be the same civilization that exists in, and has built up the east. That is what we are all aiming at, and therefore, although I thoroughly agree with the minister as to the wisdom of this clause, there should be great care in prohibiting undesirable immigrants, I certainly should like to see a generous interpretation of those clauses which permit or encourage immigration from Great Britain, because while it is desirable to prevent the settling of the west by a people unsuited for the country, and undesirable it is at the same time our duty to give every encouragement to, and not to partially prohibit or check the immigration of those people who although at first they may not fall on their feet, and succeed in their new surroundings, would, with their children, eventually build up the right kind of citizenship.
I am glad personally to see that in some respects the government's efforts are meeting with success. But let me refer to what occurred at the seventh conference of the Chambers of Commerce of the empire in Australia last year. That is a body of enormous importance not only in building up the various portions of the empire including Canada, but also in diverting capital to this country in greater amounts every year. Two or three representatives of Canada attended that conference. In the closing days the question of immigration was discussed, and the following resolution was proposed by Sir Alfred Spicer, president of the London Chamber of Commerce:
That the settlement in adequate volume of the Anglo-Saxon race in the British dominions is deserving of the constant solicitude of the home and colonial governments, who are hereby urged to consider what further or better steps than those at present exists should be taken to elaborate a general state-aided scheme at reduced rates to encourage emigration of suitable settlers under well-considered conditions.
I may remind the House that the imperial Chambers of Commerce with which various Canadian bodies are affiliated, have been working along this line for many years, from 1896 on, and they have been drawing attention not only to the need of building up Canada, Australia, and South Africa with the best types of British immigrants, but have also striven to show their own people the necessity of directing the flow of British capital to these various portions of the empire in connection with the immigration movement so as to build it up along concomitant lines. I think I will be pardoned for putting on ' Hansard ' these figures of Sir Alfred Spicer's to show the striking changes that have taken place in this direction:
In 1891, out of a total departure from the shores of the United Kingdom of 156,930 British emigrants, only 47,636 were bound for parts of the British empire, while 103,394 were destined for foreign countries-of whom 104,001 went to the United States. Fifteen years later, Sir Albert continued, in 1907, the total of British emigrants reached 395,680, of whom no fewer than 212,672 chose another part of the British empire as their destination, while 183,008 left for foreign countries-the United States claiming 170,264. So that, whereas only 30-5 per cent of the British emigrants in 1894 were retained within the empire's borders and 69-5 per cent strayed to foreign climes, in 1907 the proportions had turned round to 53'8 per cent in favour of the British empire against 46-2 per cent for all other parts of the world, an improvement in the empire's power of absorption of Britain's surplus population of no less than 23 -3 per cent. Finally, the number of emigrants to places within the empire in 1907 was nearly five-fold the number that went there in 1894, whilst the number going to foreign countries had not doubled -the actual increases between the two years being for the British empire 165,035 and for all other countries 74,614.
In that connection Sir Alfred Spicer's final remarks were:
The London chamber, therefore, considers that on imperial grounds, on commercial and financial considerations, the home and the colonial governments should do all in their power to stimulate and assist in the more rapid peopling of imperial areas, by evolving some plan in conference, encouraging, as the

resolution suggests, ' emigration of suitable settlers under well-considered conditions.'
Some discussion took place on the question of aid to immigration from Great Britain. I do think personally that there should be a generous interpretation of these clauses by the minister when he comes to deal with the type of a settler to whom Sir Alfred Spicer has been alluding. As I understand, a clause has been passed providing that no immigrant would be allowed to land here if he had been aided by money given to him or by charitable organizations. It is true we are doing some work of that kind in Great Britain, and I believe they are also in Ontario, but after all I think the minister will admit that a man who is healthy and strong, and whom there is nothing to reproach with mentally or bodily, although he might not have been able in the crowded centres of Great Britain to make his way, and save money, should be the subject of generous interpretation of our Canadian laws so as to give him a chance. After all, although he may not have the money, and although some one may have helped him, he may make the most valuable type of citizen we can get. So I suggest in closing that while we all hope for the success of this Act which I cordially say I believe is making for better things in our immigration policy, I feel there should be an exercise of wisdom in the selection of our immigration agents, and in their methods, and a broad, sane, and generous interpretation of those clauses both of encouragement, and prohibition. Without such an interpretation, and without that wisdom of appointment I do not think the Act can be a success. If it is administered in that spirit the minister can confidently expect to do a great deal more on the right lines.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As to the character of the immigration officers, I may say that we can only work with the material available, and I think it is a fair statement that our immigration officers are fairly representative of the intelligence and honesty of the people of Canada. We hope to improve the condition as it seems necessary and becomes possible. Because we have a certain condition to-day it does not follow that we should rest easy and pay no attention to the possibilities of improvement. My hon. friend may depend upon it that we recognize very thoroughly the absolute necessity of working through officials of honesty and intelligence, and that from time to time we shall take such measures as will secure us officials of that character. My hon. friend suggested that there was a good deal of misrepresentation on the part of our agents in Great Britain, as to the conditions in Canada. I do not think he is warranted in that belief. The literature that we publish for circulation in the old Mr. BURRELL.
country is very carefully prepared, and with a special view to the necessity of not raising any unreasonable or unwarranted expectations in the mind of the intending immigrant. Our principal piece of literature is the ' Atlas ' upon which I think I may say a large majority of the members of the House have complimented the department. That is the standard of the literature we circulate and on the fly leaf of all the literature we issue, except the ' Atlas ', we give notice that the only people we advise to come to Canada are the people who are going to engage in farm work or domestic service, and we warn all others to only come on such information as they may secure outside of our literature. With regard to the question of assisted immigration I have only to say that while finding no fault with any other government which see3 fit to adopt a policy of assisted immigration, our conclusion is that in Canada, and for Canada the best results are to be achieved by simple advertisement of the advantages of the country, depending uppn the attraction of those advantages to bring here the people we want. It is the spirit in the man that is more important than the frame of his person. The spirit of enterprise and determination which makes him willing to take the risks involved in coming and to raise the money for that purpose, is the most valuable asset of the immigrant-more valuable even than his physical strength. It is that part of the immigrant's character that we are not so well assured of getting when we undertake to assist him in coming to this country. We are content to find ourselves with a smaller number if we get the men of a better quality. My hon. friend has suggested that we should be lenient in the interpretation of our regulations as respects our kinsmen from the British islands. His suggestion is right and proper, and it i3 a part of our policy and administration. Let it be distinctly understood by each member of the committee upon whom rests the responsibility of legislation, that if he deems it necessary to pass a law restricting immigration the fact of that law being upon the statute-book places upon the government of the day the responsibility of enforcing its provisions. The restrictive provisions of our immigration law which are now in force, and which will be in force under this Act, mean hardship in many cases. There are heart-breaking instances, hundreds of them under its administration. But, it is the law, not of the government, but of the parliament of Canada, and it expresses the mind of our people in regard to these questions. The responsibility of the government is to carry out the will of the people thus expressed. It i3 impossible to enforce a harsh statute in a soft way. I would wish that every member of the House should appreciate the full measure of his responsibility in endorsing the dras-

tic exclusion provisions of this immigration law; he must share with the government the responsibility for the hardship which occurs under it. It would not be acting fairly by the country, and the government would stand to be condemned, if having been authorized by parliament to enforce certain exclusion provisions, the government did not' give effect to those provisions. I do not think there is any member of the House who appreciates more than I do the terrible hardships that arise under the administration of this immigration law; but under the responsibility which I hold from this House, and from the country, I have a duty to perform, and I wish to perform it, while as leniently as possible, yet as honestly and as fairly as possible, and as much in accord with the instructions of parliament as possible.

One way in which the minister can avoid these hardships of immigrants when they arrive in this country is by having the inspection made as far as possible_on the other side of the water. My hon. friend says that it is difficult to do that. It is difficult; if it were not, any one could do it, but we expect him to find a way in which it can be done. If my hon. friend saw the heart-rending scenes that take place when families are broken up on the landing of the immigrants, I think he would endeavour to find a way by which this would be done. It is a big task, but there is nothing too big for the Canadian government when it is right.

I wish to suggest that there is a certain kind of literature which the department might use with great advantage much more than it does. 1 hold in my hand a book which I believe has been got up under the direction of the Minister of Agriculture. A coov of this book should be put into the hands of every booking agent -on the other side of the ocean. Complaint has been made that certain parts of Canada have not been properly looked after in seeking for immigrants. Here is a book which gives full information in regard to the resources and productions of every province. With regard to British Columbia, it gives all particulars about minerals, the fisheries and the lumber of the province. The book is published in German, French and English. I have Tead it in the three languages, and I must say that if it had a greatei circulation, it would do a great deal oi good. Such a book is not thrown into the waste basket, but it is put into a library where it can be taken down anv time. If 200,000 copies of this book were sent abroad, I believe they would do a great deal more good than some of our agents. I have recommended it a great many times, and a great many copies have been sent
through my influence to countries where it can be read. I think this -book is much better than the atlas to which the minister has referred. Another thing 1 must say for it is that it is thoroughly accurate. It gives full particulars about our homestead regulations and about every part of Canada. I hope it will be put into much more extensive -circulation than it has been in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I shall be glad to take notice of what my hon. friend has said, and to see what we can do in the way of . circulating the- book in question; but I may say to my hon. friend that whereas the atlas which we circulate very freely costs some seven cents, I fancv that the book to which he refers, in the binding such as he has, would not cost less than 75 cents or $1; so that to circulate it in very large numbers would cost very much in comparison with what we do at present in the way of circulating literature. In regard to the inspection of immigrants on the other side of the Atlantic, I cannot change the view which I have already expressed, that it does not seem to me to be practicable. It has been suggested -here to-day that an inspection might be had by a medical officer responsible to this government who would be on the ship and who would make the inspection on the way out. That would give us a better inspection, but would not altogether _ relieve the situation of which my hon. friend has spoken, and I will admit that I do not know of any way of absolutely relieving it. We come nearest to doing so, I think, by impressing thoroughly on the steamship companies that undesirables will not be accepted. Then, in their own interest, they check them on the other side. This is a case in which too great leniency is not mercy, but cruelty, because if we exercise leniency to-day, advantage is attempted to be taken of that to-mprrow, and where! we let one undesirable in today, a dozen will have to be turned back to-morrow because of that one having been let in. I think it is more merciful to have a strict and impartial administration of the law than it would be to show leniency in special cases.

I quite agree with the hon. minister, and that is what we are trying to assist him in guarding against. If this doctor whom it is proposed to put on board the ship were put on the dock at Liverpool, he could turn back the undesirables there, and this would avoid the breaking up of families when they arrive on this side. If the minister made up his mind, I think he could find a means of having the inspection done on the otb*-side.
Section 38 agreed to.
With the consent of the committee, I would move for a reconsideration of section 37.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

Just before Mr. Speaker left the chair at six o'clock, the hon. minister moved an amendment to clause 37 requiring tourists landing at any port in Canada to show the same amount of money as an immigrant may be required to produce. I was not in the House at the moment, and I understand that this amendment went through without discussion. As representing a part of Canada very largely interested in the tourist business, I feel impelled to lay before the minister the facts, as they present themselves to me, in connection with the amendment. I do not know whether it has been the minister's privilege to visit of late the maritime provinces, but if so, he must have noticed, particularly if his visit were made during the summer months, that a very large tourist business has developed there of recent years. The business is not only very large, but very profitable, and engaged in by a very large number of people. In almost every county of the maritime provinces are a number of summer resorts where thousands of American visitors spend the summer months. To insist on such a provision as that proposed by the minister, would likely bring about a condition of things which will not be conducive to the well-being of this very profitable business, the development of which is the outcome of a great deal of time and energetic work I may say that some years ago there was a similar provision-in fact I believe it exists to-day-in the immigration laws of the United States, and I know that people from Nova Scotia going to Boston-well-to-do people who were merely going there on a visit-were held up on the docks, perhaps on a stormy day, amidst crowds of people, and compelled to declare the amount of money they carried with them. The experience was most disagreeable, many protests weie made, and as a result of this, many people refrained from travelling by the lines where they were subjected to such indignity. The fact, I think, was also brought up in this House last session that some very distinguished people entering the United States from Mexico last year, or the year before, and also people entering Buffalo from Canada were held up in this way, and some were actually turned back. They were put to a great deal of trouble and inconvenience simply because they had not the necessary amount of money in coin of the realm about their persons. These people were not immigrants in any sense of the word, but well-to-do travellers who were simply visiting the country for a short time. If there were an existing evil in this connection in Canada, if immigrants were endeavouring to pass themselves off as Mr. BICKERDIKE.
tourists, I can understand that this amendment might be necessary; but unless that condition actually exists and has become a source of evil, I do not think it advisable to place a restriction of this kind in the Act. We have been told by the hon. minister that every member of parliament must share with the government the responsibility of these restrictive measures, and that is what gives me the warrant to say here, on behalf of the maritime provinces, that it would very prejudiciously affect the tourist business in those provinces, by creating a prejudice in the minds of American tourists against this country. Suppose, for instance, that some officious officer is stationed on the dock when a steamship arrives from an American port. This man may consider it his duty to hold up every passenger, even ladies travelling with their children and without the protection of their husbands. One can easily understand how irritating it would be and how inconvenient to a lady to have to show what money she may have in her possession. Ladies travelling, as a rule, are very careful lest their money be lost or stolen, and consequently they frequently only carry m their pockets the smallest amount required. For that l-eason, if for no other, they ought not to be subjected to this serious inconvenience and indignity. Similar experiences have happened to our own people on visiting American ports and created in them much indignation and a very unfavourable impression. One can easily understand how prejudicially the enforcement of -such a position would affect in particular our tourist traffic. I strongly urge that the hon. minister would reconsider this amendment and have it struck out.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When I explained the amendment to the committee, it seemed to be well received. I thought it reasonable that while tourists are exempt from the immigration restriction, still there was no reason why they -should not show at least the amount of money which the mere immigrant would be required to have as the condition of his entering the country. Our difficulty in administering the law is that if a man says he is a tourist we cannot produce any evidence that he is not, and in uieh a case our restriction as to the possession of money would become of no effect. It was not with a desire to in any way hamper the tourist traffic or interfere with legitimate tourists that I proposed this amendment, but in order to prevent the existence of a loop hole by which the purposes of the Act might be avoided. Let me point out also that this provision does not say that the tourist must have a certain amount of money. All that it does is to authorize the Governor in Council to pass regulations in that regard. It is not required that the regulation shall be of any character _ which would tend to interfere

with tourist traffic. All we ask is that power be granted the Governor m Council by regulation rather than by statute, so that the regulations may be varied from time to time to suit the varying conditions. I can assure my hon. friend that, under this section with the amendment as proposed, there is no danger such as he anticipates, but every care will be taken in framing regulations that the ordinary travel, including the tourist travel, shall not be unduly interfered with.

I agree entirely with what my hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) has said. I myself know the inconvenience, the excessive annoyance, created by American regulations of very much the same purport as those the minister proposes to make under this Bill. Some two years ago, two respectable men employed in Hamilton, started on a trip to Buffalo. They were stopped at Niagara Falls bridge by a couple of gentlemen with stars on their shoulders, who asked them where they were going, and whether they were going to find employment in Buffalo. They said they were going to visit their friends in Buffalo-they were merely going on a trip for the day, intending to return that evening. But the officers chose to say that they did not believe these men, and in the presence of the whole trainload of people, put them off the train. Naturally, they were indignant. Of course they could have gone before an official of the United States and proved their case-as if they had been before a police magistrate-and, perhaps, might have been allowed to proceed. But they preferred to come home. They spoke to me about the matter, and I called the attention of the government to it. The government corresponded with Washington, and there were all sorts of expressions of regret, but these were of no value to these two men. They were as decent, respectable men as the minister or any member of this House. And I can only say that, if I know the minister, and he had been treated as these men were, the atmosphere would have been blue for several acres round. It was simply an outrage. No person, except under the greatest necessity, should have been exposed to such an insult. I recollect also the case of a couple of English gentlemen who sought to pass from Mexico into the United States, but were stopped and turned back because they had not the evidence to satisfy a government official. Now if the minister (Mr. Oliver) can point out that there has been any real grievance or trouble about immigrants posing as tourists, and so getting into the country, this might be a subject for consideration. But I doubt if he can mention one case of an immigrant having tried to pass himself
off as a tourist. Such a provision as is here proposed should not be on the statute-book and should not be in regulations passed by the government under which visitors coming into the country may be subjected to such insults, unless there is the gravest necessity on grounds of the public welfare. There is not a word about tourists in the Bill as he drew it. Why does he drag it in now? He should be slow to bring in such a proposal. It is an insult to tourists and visitors to say that a man may be called upon, on a public wharf or in a public railway station, to show how much money he has. You could not ask much more of a suspected pickpocket. I should be quite willing to see every regulation that is reasonable authorized, but nothing of this kind should be placed on the statute-book except under the direst necessity.
1 take it that regulations would be made under this provision of the law to provide for the admission of tourists. Otherwise, this might work hardship.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is why we do not make provision in the statute-because a measure of elasticity is required in dealing with this question. Therefore, we provide for it under regulation. We ask authority to make regulations that will be effective, that is all.

Has the hon. minister had any complaints of difficulties arising at any of the main points at which tourists enter Canada-of immigrants smuggling themselves in under the guise of tourists? I happen to represent a riding that is visited every year by many tourists, nearly all from the United States. I should be sorry to see an enactment either in this statute, or by regulation, to interfere with those coming in the summer time to enjoy our northern country. These people would feel it very keenly if they were stopped at the border and made to show that they had a certain sum of money in their pockets. Very few immigrants enter Canada by way of Niagara, I suppose. I trust that this regulation will be so made and administered that officers should not assume an arrogant air with tourists.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend may be perfectly satisfied that there will be no such regulation or administration as would have the effect he fears. The fact that there have been arbitrary actions on the part of United States officials does not at all indicate that the same action will be taken by officials on our side of the line. We handle our business in a somewhat different way. The fact that we have had exclusion officers at work for nearly two

years, with very little complaint, although they have turned back many people, is, I think, evidence that we have officers fairly competent, and not a discredit to either Canada or the government. It is not a question of administration under the Act, but a question of the Act giving sufficient power to the government to enable it to frame regulations that will be effective for the purpose desired. Our difficulty is that under this new Act, if a man claims to be a tourist, he is free of the country and can come and go as he pleases. Having given him that right by the terms of the Act, which he did not have before, I think it is only reasonable that we should have authority by regulation to see that he did not have any advantage over the ordinary immigrant.

I do not understand how the minister hopes to avoid trouble and friction* over this matter. He says it does not follow that because there has been trouble occasioned by officious officials at the United States border, the same thing is going to occur in Canada, because our officials may conduct themselves differently. Now, I believe it is true that Canadian officials are more courteous to the travelling public, and particularly to ladies, than are American officials; at the same time, I think there is a good deal of truth in the remark of David Harum that 'there is as much human nature in some people as there is in others,' and if you happen to have appointed an officious official at any place he will cause a good deal of friction and dissatisfaction before you nave got rid of him. The minister says this provision is placed in the Act merely to give him authority to make certain regulations. Well, if regulations are going to be made they will have to be carried out. We do not want to place on the statute-book any law which we are not going to live up to. If an evil exists along this line, then it may perhaps be the duty of parliament to frame this section so as to give the minister that power. But we have yet to learn from him that this evil does exist, we have yet to learn that immigrants come in to our country styling themselves as tourists. But if such a thing should occur, we have in subsection 10 of section 33 a provision which would meet that case, and which reads :
Every person who enters Canada as a tourist, or traveller, or other non-immigrant, but who ceases to be such and remains in Canada, shall forthwith report such facts to the nearest immigration officer, and shall present himself before an officer for examination under this Act, and in default of so doing he shall be liable to a fine of not more than one hundred dollars, and shall also be liable to deportation by order of a board of inquiry or officer acting as such.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Surely that provides a remedy in case any of these immigrants class themselves as tourists, and under that guise get into the country. Another difficulty arises. Supposing a man presents himself at any port and says: I am -a tourist, and the official says: No, you are an immigrant. In such a case, I presume, it would be for the individual to prove that he was a bona fide tourist. But I may say for the information of the minister, that as regards tourists coming to the maritime provinces, they would not have any difficulty in proving that they were not immigrants; at the same time it would be distasteful for them to be held ud by some official, and perhaps be required to remain for a few hours or a day until they could communicate with their friends at home. I do not think it is well that we in Canada should place such obstructions in the way of friendly intercourse between the peoples of Canada and of the United States. The class of people who come to the maritime provinces and present themselves as tourists come from the United States. If they wdre immigrants actually seeking entry into Canada, they would not be likely to come to the maritime provinces, I presume the west would be their goal. As regards people coming from European ports and presenting themselves at the maritime provinces port, I think the minister may rest assured that no person disembarking from a steamship and presenting himself as a tourist, would do so if, as a matter of fact, he was only an immigrant. It would be well known by the officials of the ship that he was an immigrant and not a tourist. For all these reasons I do not think the minister should press this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend and others who have spoken have asked what instances there were of the necessity of this provision. There are no instances, because the necessity for it has not yet arisen, and will not arise until this Act comes into force. Under the Act we are operating under now, a tourist is a person who is passing through Canada, and such person would be free to pass without the production of the money qualifications. But under this Bill we propose to give the tourist who comes to tour in Canada the privilege of coming in as a non-immigrant, a privilege which he has not under the present Act. Under the present Aci and under the present regulations every man, whether he be a tourist or an immigrant, may be required to produce the $25. Now we propose by the new Act to relieve the tourist in Canada from the disabilities of an immigrant; but in doing so it seems to me that it is not unfair that while relieving him from disability in some particulars we should protect ourselves By regulations in the case of the money qualification.

v
If the hon. gentleman were going to England and passed through Niagara Falls, and were held up there to show how much money he had in his pocket, I think he wolud be very angry and indignant.

Will the minister give [DOT]his reasons for inserting that provision in the Act and yet declining an amendment moved last evening to prevent the coming into Canada of that very class of immigrants? That is to say of any person who advocates the overthrow by force or violence of the government of - Great Britain or Canada or any part of the British dominions.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The reason is the same as the one I gave last night, that the question whether the applicant for entrance to Canada is of this class or not in the large majority of cases cannot by any possibility be settled at the port of entry. The only way we can decide that is on evidence secured, and we secure that evidence after the man has come into Canada and on the establishment of the facts we are entitled to take certain action. Although the provision is in the United States statute it is not effective, it does not protect the United States from the entrance of all these classes of people and I do not think there is any object in burdening the statute with a provision that is on the face of it absolutely ineffective.

The minister's ideas of an Act of parliament then is that it may be capable of proof, and he may know that a man is of the character and class that will justify his expulsion from the country, but although he knows that he will let him enter.

The minister said last night that although this provision to exclude anarchists and those who favour the overthrow of government from the United States was on the American statute-book . it did not prevent the entry into that country of that undesirable class ol immigrants. I have looked the matter uo and so far as I can ascertain that provision was enacted in the United 'States in 1903; it may have been in a previous year, but so far as I can ascertain it was then first embodied in the statute. The United States have had much more experience than we have in immigration and if we fail to profit by the mistakes which they made in the earlier days of their immigration we are open to censure. They found in time that an undesirable class of immigrants were entering the country and they put on their statute-book a regulation stopping at the very gateway of their country that undesirable class of immigrants. The minister says that the Act has not excluded
these people. I am willing to accept his statement up to a certain point, I am willing to say it will not always be possible to prove that a man is an anarchist, but I say that according to the Bill now before us a man may be an avowed anarchist, he may come to Canada and there will be no possibility of excluding him. lie will have the right of entry into this country, and after he has entered, then, forsooth, the minister turns around and, under section 41, the machinery of the Act is set in motion, an investigation is had, learned gentlemen sit on the case and perhaps an order is made to deport this undesirable person from the country. I say that is locking the stable door after the horse is stolen, and it is not profiting as we should do by the early mistakes of the United States. There are several classes of undesirables whom the minister desires to exclude, but it is not always easy to prove that immigrants are of the classes mentioned, for instance persons with a loathsome disease or a disease dangerous to the public health or persons convicted of any crime involving moral turpitude. These provisions are in the Act, but the minister does not say that we can prove that immigrants are of these classes. To leave the Act in such shape that it is not possible to refuse admission to an avowed anarchist, although we have the machinery to deport him afterwards, is contrary to all rules of reason and every principle of common sense.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot agree with my hon. friend. When we undertake to interfere with the right of expression of opinion, the right of personal liberty, to question the right of men to say what they please, we should only take action when we have it within our power to establish the facts. I do not think it is right or reasonable that we should declare a man to be of these classes until we are in a position to know and to prove it, and we can only do that, in the large majority of cases, after he comes inside our country.
On section 42, deportation of head of family.

Subsection 5 says that where the head of a family is ordered to be deported all dependent members of the family may be deported at the same time. It seems to me that, if the intention is that all the members of the family shall be deported with the head of the family, that may be a very severe and harsh regulation. It of course might turn out that if the other members of the family were permitted to remain in the country they would be able to provide for themselves. I have not examined the section very closely, but it seems to me there may be a little confusion

in that sentence and the next following one in the same section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The intention is, as I believe it is expressed here, that if the head of a family has to be deported, those who are dependent upon him should go with him. It is not said that they shall go, but that they may go. The next sentence deals with the -case of the head of a family who has failed to support a dependent member of that family. We consider such a person an undesirable -citizen, and we provide that if the dependent requires to be deported, the head of the family upon whom that individual is dependent should go out with him.

If the minister will allow me to refer to section 39, it seems to me that should be left out altogether. It provides that if an immigrant comes from a foreign country through another foreign country to Canada-say an immigrant comes from Italy through the United States to this country-the minister can compel the steamship company that brought that immigrant from Italy to New York to deport him from Canada. Surely the minister would have no control over steamships that bring immigrants from one foreign country to another foreign -country. Therefore I would think it better to leave the clause out altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is quite true that if a company had no Canadian connection, nothing could be done; but the purpose is to compel the company to make the deportation when it has a Canadian connection.
Has the minister ever had an instance that could be brought under this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, many instances. Although there are many cases which for the reasons stated by my hon. friend this provision will not cover, there are other cases which it will cover, and it is very desirable from our point of view that we should have this provision.
On section 43-detention of certain prisoners for deportation.

Is the minister particularly anxious to make the limit three years? I observe that Dr. C. K. Clark, who is the head of the insane hospital at Toronto, suggests four years, which he says will afford better opportunity for thorough investigation, and make the provision more efficient.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
At present the term is two years. We wish to extend that to three years, for obvious reasons, and partly because that is the term in the United States; and it is convenient, in the interchange of undesirables, that our regu-Mr. JAMESON.
lations should, when it is right and proper, be the same. I would very much prefer that the term might be allowed to remain as it is in the Act for the persent. The extension we are making is an improvement to that extent from my hon. friend's point of view.

I think, from reading the American report, that the American officials are not satisfied with three years, and would like the term lengthened. I cannot see why there should be any limit of time in regard to getting rid of an undesirable. There is an insane hospital in Montreal where 39 per cent of the inmates are foreign-born, and in the Toronto insane hospital in 1906, 1907 and 1908, out of 424 inmates, 210 were foreign-bom. If the term were longer, many of these might be deported, and I think we should have a right to deport undesirables at any time we see fit.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have provided elsewhere in the Act that Canadian domicile shall be acquired by residence of three years. I think it reasonable that if a man lives in the country for a certain length of time he should have certain recognized rights.
On section 45,
Every person ordered to be deported under this Act who has been brought to Canada by ship, shall be reconveyed free of charge by the same transportation company which brought him to Canada, from the place in Canada where he is being detained or held for deportation to the port of embarkation whence he came to Canada, and in the same manner as to passage accommodation by which he was brought to Canada; and similarly every such person brought to Canada by a railway train or other vehicle shall, subject to the regulations under sections 31 and 32 of this Act, be reconveyed free of charge by the transportation company which carried him to the place in Canada where he is rejected or where he is being detained for deportation to the place in the country whence he was brought or to the country of his birth or citizenship.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The intention is that the company which brought the undesirable out shall have to take him back free of charge to the man himself as well as to the government. As the section stands, it requires that the steamship company shall take him from the place in Canada where he may be detained to the ocean port where he landed, and thence to the original port of embarkation. The steamship companies object to this. They say they are willing to take the deport back to the port at which they embarked him, but that the railway company which carried him to the place where he is detained should bring him back to the port. In accordance with that view I beg to move that section 45 be

amended by striking out all the words after ' the ' in the sixth line to, and including the word ' Canada,' in the tenth line, and substituting the following:	The railway
company or companies which brought him to the place in Canada where he is being detained for deportation to the ocean port where he was landed, or the nearest available winter ocean port, as may be directed by the board of inquiry, and thence he shall be conveyed free of charge to the port of embarkation whence he came, and in such manner as to passage, and condition as may be directed by the officer in charge.

It will be very difficult to show what railway company carried him from the port of landing. When an immigrant lands on the dock, a record is kept of him, and it is known by what ship he arrived; but once released, he is free to chose any railway he pleases by which to leave that port.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The point is well taken. I see the difficulty, but on the other hand the steamship companies hold that they should not be required to pay the expense of inland transportation for which they were not responsible, and for which they received no benefit. I do not wish that any interest in the country should be harshly dealt with, and I propose this amendment in deference to the contention of the steamship companies, although there is the difficulty my bon. friend suggests.

I am bound to say that I approve of the section as it is. A steamship company, which has the right of inspection, and selection of these people, should take the responsibility. It is unfair to a railway company, which takes a man in perfect good faith, to be compelled to pay the expense of bringing him back. That man is as free to come, and go as anybody else, and the innocent railway company, which is not required to have an inspection of him, has to transport him back to the place where the steamship company can take him up. It is the duty of the steamship company to see that the immigrants they bring out are the right class. They have been making a lot of money out of this business, and if reports are true, and if the stringent measures in this Bill are warranted, these companies are not very careful in their selection. If they will bring undesirables to this>
country who have to be deported, they should bear all the expense.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is a great deal of force in what my hon. friend says. If I might withdraw for the moment my amendment, I wish to move another amendment to the wording which will make the section more effective, and we might have an opportunity of discussing the amendment I 186
am asking to withdraw before the Bill comes out of committee. I wish to give due consideration to all the interests concerned. Yet I feel very strongly the force of the arguments my hon. friend has presented. I ask for leave, therefore, to withdraw the motion, and to move that the words ' the same,' be struck out, and that ' such,' be substituted, and that the words ' by which he was brought to Canada,' be struck out, and ' as may be directed by the officer in charge,' be substituted. As the Bill is printed, the deport must be taken back with the same accommodation as that with which he was brought. Sometimes, this is not desirable. So, instead of making it mandatory that the steamship shall take him back in the same class as that in which he came out, the matter is left to the discretion of the superintendent of immigration.	__
That is better than the other amendment that the minister has suggested, but this may be a little tough on the deport.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Sometimes a man who has come out first-class falls on evil days and is not a proper subject for first-class transportation going back. I think it is fair to leave the matter to the discretion of the superintendent.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendments agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I would like to have the section as amended stand until the end of the Bill, so that we may consider it further.
On section 48-penalty on transportation company permitting escape of persons ordered to be deported; duty to notify immigration officer when such person escapes.

Failure to notify renders one liable to a penalty of not more than $20, and not less than $10 for each offence. But for negligence, or connivance leading to escape, the penalty is not more than $500 and not less than $50. Should there be this difference in the penalties for practically the same cffence?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are hardly the same offence. One is negligence in allowing escape, and the other is negligence in notifying.
But the person who allows a deport to escape is likely to fail to report the fact of that escape. It seems to me that it would be better to stiffen up the penalty.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The party who is guilty of both negligence in allowing to escapee and failure to report is guilty of both offences and liable to both penalties.
But, in order to impose the larger penalty, it would be necessary to prove both offences, and that is not contemplated under the section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The man who has knowledge of the escape may not be the man who is responsible for it. The man who is responsible is liable to the large penalty, while the man who has knowledge but is not responsible, yet fails to report, is subject to the smaller penalty.

Has the minister considered in what form this manifest is to be, that is, whether the manifest which has to be presented will contain the names and description of all the passengers, or whether there will be a number of manifests? According to the regulations in the United States, these manifests are so arranged that they do not include more than thirty names, and in that way it is possible to arrange the passengers int-o classes. How does the minister propose to carry out that section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The provisions of this section are practically in effect under the existing Act. I am not familiar with the form of manifest, but there is a form which complies with the requirements of the section.
On section 51, manifest of outbound passengers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The steamship companies complain in regard to this provision that the manifest is not complete until the vessel has actually sailed, and to require the completion of the manifest so as to hand it to the immigration officer before the vessel sails, would unduly delay the sailing. This is merely a provision to keep tally of the neople who are going out of the country with a view to checking them as they come back, and it is proposed that the manifest shall be produced on the return voyage. In order to meet the case, I would move that the words ' before clearance has been given to such vessel ' in subsection 1, be struck out, and the words ' on the return voyage of such vessel to Canada ' be substituted therefor.
Does this relate to vessels which ply between maritime province ports and United States ports, or does it mean vessels of the transatlantic lines?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As it reads, it would be applicable to both, but it is not intended to apply to both. The principle purpose is not in regard to Atlantic passengers, but to Pacific passengers. There is a difficulty about the identification of Asiatics, who claim entrance as returning passengers, and we want to have a tally of the outgoing Asiatics, so that we may have better opportunities of checking the incoming ones who claim to be returning to Canada. It is really with a view to that traffic that we desire this provision.

At the same time, does not the minister think that while he may Mr, .1AMESON.
be intending to erect this section against that class of steamship lines, it will also apply to steamship lines on the Atlantic waters as well? Now, although perhaps this is not the occasion or the proper time,
I want to say something with respect to the passenger traffic which is carried on between the maritime ports and Americap ports. At the present time, ships which ply between these ports are overloaded to such a degree that I think they are positively unsafe; they are overloaded to such an extent that the people cannot get proper accommodation, and some day there will be a serious accident attended with great loss of life. I think these companies require to have a license which limits the number of passengers thev are entitled to carry. But they do not declare the number of passengers which they carry, and after they leave the dock, it is reported next day in the papers after sailing that such and such a steamer left such and such a port in Canada for such -and such a port-in the United States, with say 500 cases of lobsters and about 600 passengers. I am told that when they get near the limited number of passengers they are entitled to carry, then only about one in five of the passengers is counted as they go on board. In that way the ships are overloaded to such an extent as not only to produce discomfort to the passengers, but to involve great danger of accident, in which some of the -pas'sengers, in -all likelihood, would be lost. Perhaps this is a matter that comes under the purview of the Marine Depart-mest, but whichever department it belongs to should see that when the vessel receives the number of passengers she is entitled to carry, no more should be allowed to go on. At present the officers winl^ at that provision of the law, and there is a great deal of dissatisfaction and fear in the minds of the travelling public that serious accidents will occur.
On section 51, manifest of outbound passengers, proviso, re exemption of vessels between Canada and Newfoundland, or the United States.

That section should properly be aimed at the very condition I spoke of, and yet I have no doubt that the steamship companies wall apply for and obtain such an exemption from the requirements of the section that the safety of the travelling public will not be conserved. I think the minister should consider that, and I would be glad to have the section stand in order that he may look into it further, and he may then see as I do that there is necessity to protect the lives of people travelling by these lines-.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This Bill is to deal with immigration, not with navigation. Necessarily the two questions overlap at times. It is because the trade between the mari-

time provinces and the New England states is not an immigration trade that the vessels engaged in that trade are expressly exempted from the provisions of the section which, as I have said, was intended to apply particularly to Asiatic trade. The condition to which my hon. friend objects is a matter for the consideration of the Department of Marine, and he would find his remedy there for the condition he mentions and not in connection with the Bill regarding immigration.
On section 59-proportionate number of passengers to area of decks.

Is there at present any inspection of vessels coming to Canadian ports, in reference to the accommodation provided for immigrants? Not very long ago there was a rumour in the United States that all was not well on these steamships, and a lady who represented either a protection society or was correspondent of a newspaper crossed and recrossed the Atlantic in the steerage. She reported that the conditions were positively revolting, and that although for years there had been a law which was supposed to be carried out for the protection of steerage passengers, the people were herded like cattle, there was insufficient provision for cleanliness, the ventilation was deficient, and the general conditions surrounding steerage travel 'degrading. Is there a thorough inspection of steamships arriving at Canadian ports to ensure protection for the immigrants? I do not mean a casual supervision which might take place after the ship is cleaned up, but have any of the officials of the department actually experienced the conditions prevailing during a voyage across the ocean in the steerage? Is it the duty of the department to see that all the comfort and protection that is contemplated by this Act shall be extended to steerage passengers?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Our agents at Liverpool, London, and Glasgow are instructed to inspect every immigrant vessel leaving these ports, and to report upon its condition. In the voyages I have made myself across the Atlantic I have taken occasion to inspect the steerage accommodation, and I have found the conditions very good. Our effort is to secure the best conditions possible under all the circumstances, and the evidence is that the conditions have materially improved within recent years upon all vessels, and while the accommodation on the older ships may not be all that is desirable, on the more recently built vessels the most fastidious could not complain of the accommodation which is given at the price at which it is given. It is really a credit to the companies and a credit to civilization.

I can understand that when the minister is on board one of these 1864
ships the officers would have everything in first-class shape. But the fact that the minister found everything right would not convey to me any assurance that at other times there may not be undesirable surroundings for the immigrants. I would suggest to the minister that he should have some trustworthy person make an actual steerage trip across the Atlantic and back without the knowledge of the steamship companies so that he might experience the actual conditions which prevail. That would be a practical way of testing whether the steamship companies are living up to the laws. There have been complaints made by immigrants from time to time that the accommodation afforded them was not what they were led to expect when they purchased their tickets. I know instances of that sort, and I dare say we all know of such instances. Of course, these complaints may not have been well founded; but Canada is now doing a large business in this way, and it seems to me only right and proper, if he can, that the minister should make an effort, by some person on whom he can rely, and whom the steamship companies will not suspect, to ascertain what conditions actually prevail under ordinary circumstances.

The hon. member for Digby has evidently given this matter a great deal of consideration judging by the amount of time he has consumed in the last three or four days in discussing it. But I would like to ask him to state, as a result of the minute examination he has made, how the minister is going to control a shipping company that has its head office in London or Berlin, and that makes a contract to bring out several hundred people to Canada. These people pay their money and take the chqice of the line on which they come out. Will he tell me how the Minister of the Interior or his officials are going to control such a company?

The committee is now considering' clause 59 which prescribes just -what the conditions of these ships shall be. If the government of Canada or the minister has no control over the matter, and any Act of the parliament of Canada relating to it is not workable and -cannot be enforced, why does the minister include that section in this Bill?

The minister may make regulations and employ inspectors, and the department might go to one of these-companies and say, unless you comply with certain requirements that we set up, we will use our influence to allot the next batch of immigrants who come out to another steamship line; but I would like to know how he can control a contract made by a company controlled in Great Britain or in Germany.
-'5879

I think the question which the hon. gentleman is struggling with will be made clear to his mind if he will read this section a little carefully. He knows, as every other hon. gentleman in this House knows, that if there is an -evil existing, if as a matter of fact these steamship companies are not giving accommodation or the treatment they should give, and nothing is known of the fact, it is going to continue, and there will be no end to it; but if it becomes public, if the newspapers take it up, as they would, and if the minister sends one of his officers to inspect the voyage and report on the facts as they exist, I have not the slightest doubt that with the penalties provided by the Act and the publicity, that steamship company would bring about a reformation.
Suppose they do not, what then?

If they do that, they will be debarred by public opinion from receiving any considerable amount of traffic. My hon. friend knows that where there are competing lines, as there are across the Atlantic to-day, if one line is held up as not giving a satisfactory service, while another is doing so, the evil will largely correct itself, and the penalties should complete the cure.

It is just as I thought. The hon. gentleman is admitting that the minister has no jurisdiction at all over these companies. He thinks that publicity will cure the evil. I only interfered to show that the hon. gentleman has taken up an enormous amount of time and has accomplished nothing. I would like to see some business done in this House tomight.
I would like to ask the minister if he accedes to the view of the hon. gentleman sitting beside him, that he has no jurisdiction whatever over these companies?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What I said, when the question was raised first, was that we had made an inspection of the immigrant vessels when they were leaving the port of embarkation, and that we used such endeavours as were within our power to bring about improvements in the conditions of the immigrant passengers. That is what we have been doing constantly during several years past, and we think we have achieved some beneficial results. So far as my knowledge goes, the conditions are certainly more favourable on the steamships recently built over what prevailed a few years ago.
If the steamship company does not comply with the regulations, what step will the minister take?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The provisions are laid down in the Act. We presume by the Act to impose certain penalties.
The hon. gentleman at the minister's right says he has no jurisdiction at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not able to answer the question, because, so far as I know, we have not undertaken to enforce these penalties. So I do not know whether our law in that respect is defective or not.
Would you not try if you had a case of that kind occur?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.
Then you think you have the power?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are assuming that we have the power. This section is_ a legacy coming down from time immemorial in the legislation of parliament. It was adopted in the Immigration Act now in force and transferred from that to the prelent Bill, simply because it was in the old statute.

I do not think any company will try to evade these things if the minister tells them that if they do he will enforce the law. They are very anxious to do the business, and they know well that if they interefere with the immigration department they will get into serious trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have ways and means outside the letter of this statute, but as to what the effect of this statute may be, I am not prepared to give an opinion.
On section 75, officers to wear uniform when on duty.
Is this the same as under the existing law?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, neither this section nor section 74, providing how uniforms shall be provided for the immigration officers, is in the present Act.
Are these uniforms furnished by the department or by the officials? Also will the minister tell us something of their appearance?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These provisions are not yet in force.

I think it has been the custom of the immigration department for years to furnish uniforms for its officers. At Halifax, Quebec, and other places that has been done, and done to a very extravagant extent. These officers have had as much as two or three suits a year sometimes. I remember that, some time ago, I took the trouble to look into this

matter. The minister should be able to state offhand whether he intends to furnish uniforms or not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that we did not provide them, but I said there was no provision in the present law on that subject. We think it better to have it in the statute, and in providing that the officer shall be required to pay one-third, we think we have arrived at an arrangement which will tend to check undue extravagance in uniforms. I think we all agree that it is right that these officers should be in uniforms, that the public may know who they are, and what their authority is.
I understood the minister to say he did not know whether he was furnishing uniforms or whether that was the intention.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What I meant in that connection was that I did not know whether we would furnish the uniforms or whether the men would get them on their order. But the provision as to paying will be governed by section 74-that one-third of the cost shall be charged to the officer.
The minister can tell us how it has been the custom to furnish these uniforms. Would the officer go to some tailor, and simply pay what the tailor charged?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer that definitely. I could explain more definitely if it were a question on the estimates of the Immigration Department, and I had the officer of the department here to advise me. I think the uniforms used now are ordered at each place where they are required-that is, uniforms for the officers in Halifax are ordered at Halifax, and so on. I do not think there is a general contract.
The prices heretofore paid have been different in different places.

Why is it specified that one-third of the cost be charged to these men? In the penitentiaries, for instance, are the guards charged one-third of the cost of their uniforms? Why not have uniformity in regard to your uniforms?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We desire to have uniformity in the department. The reason why we have adopted this idea of requiring the official to pay for a portion of the cost is to check his asking for too many uniforms. It may be an innovation so far as the government service is concerned, but we think it a proper innovation, and ask the committee to adopt it.
If it is a good principle in this case, why not adopt it in other branches of the service?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is a difference between an immigration officer, and, say, a penitentiary guard.
Or a customs or excise officer?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is a greater resem- -blance there. I do not know what arrangement is made in the Customs Department, but I think the committee should sanction this proposal in regard to the: immigration service.

Does not the minister
think that fifty per cent would be a more effective check?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
